::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Fine particulate matter ($\text{PM}_{2.5}$) is the mass, in micrograms per cubic meter of air, of airborne particles that pass a size cut at about 2.5 micrometers (µm) in diameter. The cut sorts particles by size, not by what they are made of, and it sits near the dip between two groups of particles in the air. Equal mass can hide very different particle counts: 15 µg/m³ of 0.1 µm particles holds about 19,000 particles per cm³, while the same mass of 2.5 µm particles holds about 1.2. Read a PM2.5 value as total fine mass over an averaging time, and ask what the air contains before you compare two numbers.
:::

## A sieve, not a substance

Particulate matter (PM) is the mix of solid and liquid specks that hang in air. The "2.5" in PM2.5 names a size limit. A sampler at the inlet of a monitor lets smaller particles through and blocks larger ones, and the instrument weighs what it collects. The result is a mass per volume of air, in µg/m³.

Size here is judged by how a particle falls. Take a sphere of density 1 g/cm³ that falls at the same speed as the particle in still air. Its diameter is the particle's aerodynamic diameter.[^hinds] A dense particle can be physically smaller than a light one and still fall like a larger particle, so the sieve sorts by how particles move.

The rule that set the standard defines PM2.5 as particles with an aerodynamic diameter at or below a nominal 2.5 µm.[^fr1997] The word "nominal" matters. The cut is a specified size, not a sharp wall. Particles near 2.5 µm are only partly collected, and the inlet's 50% point marks the size where half get through. The sieve does not care about chemistry. Soot, sulfate, dust and salt all count if they are small enough.

## Particles come in modes

Airborne particles do not spread evenly across sizes. They cluster into groups called modes. The fine mode holds particles below about 1 µm. These form mostly from combustion and from gases that react in the air.[^seinfeld] The coarse mode holds larger particles, such as wind-blown dust and sea spray, that come from mechanical processes.

Between the two modes the mass is low. The 1997 rule states that the diameter reflecting this mass minimum typically lies between 1 and 3 µm, and that a sampling cut point should separate fine particles somewhere in that range.[^fr1997] The choice of a specific size, such as 2.5 µm, is a policy judgment. Any single cut only approximates the true fine mass, because some particles on either side of the dip are misclassified.

Each mode is a bell curve on a logarithmic size scale, which statisticians call a lognormal shape. Its volume median diameter sets where it sits. Its geometric standard deviation, a spread factor, sets how wide it is: a value of 2 means about two-thirds of the volume lies between half and twice the median. Figure 1 plots dV/dlogD, the volume of particles in each logarithmic size slice, so the area under a mode is its share of the volume. Its modes are illustrative, not measured data.

::: {.sim-card}
#### Modes and the PM2.5 and PM10 cuts

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Illustrative lognormal modes in log10(D), volume-weighted. Not measured.
modeShape = (D, Dg, sg, amp) => amp * Math.exp(-0.5 * ((Math.log10(D) - Math.log10(Dg)) / Math.log10(sg)) ** 2)

grid = d3.range(-2, 2.0001, 0.01).map(x => 10 ** x)
fineRaw = grid.map(D => modeShape(D, 0.3, 2, 1))
coarseRaw = grid.map(D => modeShape(D, 6, 2.2, 0.6))
totalRaw = grid.map((D, i) => fineRaw[i] + coarseRaw[i])
peak = Math.max(...totalRaw)

fineRows = grid.map((D, i) => ({D, v: fineRaw[i] / peak}))
coarseRows = grid.map((D, i) => ({D, v: coarseRaw[i] / peak}))
totalRows = grid.map((D, i) => ({D, v: totalRaw[i] / peak}))

Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 360,
  marginLeft: 56,
  marginBottom: 48,
  style: {background: "transparent"},
  x: {
    type: "log", label: "Particle diameter, D (µm)", domain: [0.01, 100],
    ticks: [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],
    tickFormat: d => d < 1 ? `${Math.round(d * 1000)} nm` : `${d} µm`
  },
  y: {label: "Relative dV/dlogD", domain: [0, 1.05], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([2.5, 10], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.line(totalRows, {x: "D", y: "v", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.line(fineRows, {x: "D", y: "v", stroke: "#38bdf8", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.line(coarseRows, {x: "D", y: "v", stroke: "#f59e0b", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.text([{D: 0.3, v: 1.0, t: "fine mode"}], {x: "D", y: "v", text: "t", dy: -10, fill: "#38bdf8"}),
    Plot.text([{D: 6, v: 0.6, t: "coarse mode"}], {x: "D", y: "v", text: "t", dy: -10, fill: "#f59e0b"}),
    Plot.text([{D: 30, v: 0.04, t: "total"}], {x: "D", y: "v", text: "t", dy: -8, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.text([{D: 2.5, v: 0.85, t: "PM2.5 cut"}], {x: "D", y: "v", text: "t", dx: -6, textAnchor: "end", fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.text([{D: 10, v: 0.85, t: "PM10 cut"}], {x: "D", y: "v", text: "t", dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: "currentColor"})
  ]
})
```

**Figure 1.** Relative volume size distribution, dV/dlogD, against particle diameter on a log axis, for illustrative modes (fine: volume median 0.3 µm, geometric standard deviation 2; coarse: 6 µm, 2.2; coarse amplitude 0.6). Solid curves: the total and its two modes, scaled so the total peaks at 1. Dashed vertical rules: the PM2.5 cut at 2.5 µm and the PM10 cut at 10 µm. The modes are illustrative. The evidence that the mass minimum lies between 1 and 3 µm is the 1997 rule,[^fr1997] not this figure.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How the mode curves are built

Each mode is a lognormal shape in $\log_{10} D$: $f(D) = A \exp\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\log_{10} D - \log_{10} D_g}{\log_{10} \sigma_g}\right)^2\right]$, where $D_g$ is the volume median diameter, $\sigma_g$ the geometric standard deviation and $A$ the amplitude. The fine mode uses $D_g = 0.3$ µm, $\sigma_g = 2$, $A = 1$; the coarse mode uses $D_g = 6$ µm, $\sigma_g = 2.2$, $A = 0.6$. These values are chosen to show the shape, not taken from a measured site. The total is the sum of the two modes, divided by its peak.
:::

Why does the cut matter? The mass on the fine side of the dip is mostly combustion and chemistry. Particles on the coarse side are mostly dust and sea spray. A cut near the dip keeps most of the fine mass and leaves out most of the coarse mass. The agency also weighed consistency with the community health studies, the limited intrusion of coarse particles, and the availability of monitoring technology.[^fr1997]

## Where particles land in the body

Particle size decides where particles deposit in the airways. Large particles mostly stop in the nose and upper airways. Smaller particles reach deeper into the lungs.[^hinds] Deep-lung deposition does not rise steadily as particles shrink, so "smaller reaches deeper" is a general rule, not an exact law. Fine particles, which reach the deep lung, are the health reason for a fine-particle cut.

## How the standard was set

The 1997 rule added PM2.5 standards next to the older standard for PM10, particles up to about 10 µm. It set the annual standard at 15 µg/m³ and the 24-hour standard at 65 µg/m³.[^fr1997] Those levels have since been tightened: in 2024 the agency lowered the annual standard from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³.[^fr2024] Among the studies the agency weighed was the Harvard Six Cities study. Its researchers followed 8,111 adults in six US cities for 14 to 16 years. After adjusting for smoking and other risk factors, the most polluted city had a mortality-rate ratio of 1.26 (95% confidence interval 1.08 to 1.47) compared with the least polluted city. Mortality was most strongly associated with fine particulates, including sulfates.[^dockery]

This is an association across cities, not proof that one component kills. The authors could not rule out unmeasured risk factors, and the pollution they measured was a mixture associated with fine particulates.

## Mass hides number and makeup

A mass concentration says how much material is in the air. It does not say how many particles carry it. Mass scales with the cube of diameter, so a few large particles can carry the same mass as a huge number of small ones.

Take 15 µg/m³ of spheres with an assumed density of 1.5 g/cm³, a round value chosen for illustration. If every particle is 0.1 µm across, the air holds about 19,000 particles per cm³. If every particle is 1 µm, it holds about 19 per cm³. If every particle is 2.5 µm, it holds about 1.2 per cm³. The mass is the same in all three cases, but the count differs by a factor of 1,000 across a tenfold change in size.

Figure 2 lets you vary the mass and the physical diameter. The density is fixed at 1.5 g/cm³ and the particles are assumed to be spheres of one size. The widget uses physical diameter, while the sieve sorts by aerodynamic diameter. For a density of 1.5 g/cm³, the aerodynamic diameter of a compact sphere is larger than its physical diameter by about $\sqrt{1.5} \approx 1.22$ times, in the size range where Stokes drag (the resistance of still air to a slow sphere) applies.[^hinds] So a 2.5 µm aerodynamic cut passes particles of about 2.0 µm physical diameter.

::: {.sim-card}
#### Same mass, how many particles?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof massUg = Inputs.range([5, 100], {value: 15, step: 1, label: "PM2.5 mass (µg/m³)"})
viewof logD = Inputs.range([-1.3, 0.4], {value: -1, step: 0.05, label: "Physical diameter (µm, log₁₀ scale)"})

rho = 1.5   // g/cm³, fixed
// 1 µg/m³ = 1e-12 g/cm³; d in µm → cm is × 1e-4
countPerCm3 = (M, d) => (M * 1e-12) / (rho * Math.PI * (d * 1e-4) ** 3 / 6)

dUm = 10 ** logD
nNow = countPerCm3(massUg, dUm)
n25 = countPerCm3(massUg, 2.5)
fmtCount = v => v >= 100 ? Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US") : v.toFixed(1)

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  <div class="sim-readout">
    <div class="sim-readout-label">Particles per cm³ at ${dUm.toFixed(2)} µm</div>
    <div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:#38bdf8">${fmtCount(nNow)}</div>
  </div>
  <div class="sim-readout">
    <div class="sim-readout-label">Particles per cm³ at 2.5 µm, same mass</div>
    <div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:#f59e0b">${fmtCount(n25)}</div>
  </div>
</div>
<p>The chosen size holds ${Math.round((2.5 / dUm) ** 3).toLocaleString("en-US")} times as many particles as 2.5 µm spheres of the same mass.</p>`
```

**Figure 2.** Count of spheres per cm³ for a PM2.5 mass of 5 to 100 µg/m³ at a chosen physical diameter from about 0.05 to 2.5 µm, with density fixed at 1.5 g/cm³. Count is $N = M / (\rho \pi d^3 / 6)$. The ratio to the 2.5 µm count is $(2.5 / d)^3$, independent of mass.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Counting particles from mass

A single sphere of diameter $d$ and density $\rho$ has mass $\rho \pi d^3 / 6$. If $M$ is the mass per volume of air, the number per volume is $N = M / (\rho \pi d^3 / 6)$. For $M$ in g/cm³, $\rho$ in g/cm³ and $d$ in cm, $N$ is in cm⁻³. A concentration of 1 µg/m³ equals $10^{-12}$ g/cm³, and 1 µm equals $10^{-4}$ cm.

With $M = 15\text{ µg/m}^3 = 1.5 \times 10^{-11}\text{ g/cm}^3$ and $\rho = 1.5\text{ g/cm}^3$, the three worked counts are $N(0.1\text{ µm}) = 19{,}099\text{ cm}^{-3}$, $N(1\text{ µm}) = 19.1\text{ cm}^{-3}$ and $N(2.5\text{ µm}) = 1.2\text{ cm}^{-3}$. The ratio $N(0.1)/N(1) = 1{,}000$ follows directly from the $d^3$ term.
:::

Mass also hides makeup. Two samples with the same PM2.5 can differ in chemistry, in toxicity, and in how their particles were made. The primary and secondary origins of fine particles are covered in [the previous post](primary-and-secondary-aerosols.qmd). For aerosols as the seeds of cloud droplets, see [what is an aerosol](what-is-an-aerosol.qmd).

## What this means for you

Read a PM2.5 value as total fine mass over an averaging time, such as one day or one year. It does not tell you how many particles are present, how big they are, or what they are made of. Before you compare two places or two days, ask what made the number. Dust, smoke, and sulfate-rich haze can give the same mass with different counts and different health effects.

Low-cost sensors need the same caution. A sensor that counts particles estimates mass by assuming a size and a density, so a wrong assumption shifts the result. Humidity matters too, because some particles take up water, and the water adds to the weight of the sample. Monitors, sensors and satellites are the subject of a later part of this series.

## Key takeaways

- PM2.5 is the mass, in µg/m³, of particles with an aerodynamic diameter at or below a nominal 2.5 µm. The cut sorts by size, not by chemistry.
- The 2.5 µm cut sits near the mass minimum between the fine and coarse modes, which the 1997 rule places between 1 and 3 µm. The exact cut is a policy judgment.
- PM2.5 was chosen because fine particles reach deeper into the lungs, and because cohort studies such as Six Cities tied fine particulate pollution to death rates.
- Equal PM2.5 mass does not imply equal particle count, composition or harm. At fixed mass, the count rises with the inverse cube of diameter.

[^fr1997]: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. National ambient air quality standards for particulate matter. *Fed. Regist.* **62**, 38652–38760 (1997). https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/1997/07/18/97-18577/national-ambient-air-quality-standards-for-particulate-matter
[^fr2024]: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Reconsideration of the national ambient air quality standards for particulate matter. *Fed. Regist.* **89**, 16202 (6 March 2024). https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2024-02637

[^dockery]: Dockery, D. W. et al. An association between air pollution and mortality in six U.S. cities. *N. Engl. J. Med.* **329**, 1753–1759 (1993). https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199312093292401

[^seinfeld]: Seinfeld, J. H. & Pandis, S. N. *Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics: From Air Pollution to Climate Change* 3rd edn (Wiley, 2016). Book; no DOI.

[^hinds]: Hinds, W. C. *Aerosol Technology: Properties, Behavior, and Measurement of Airborne Particles* 2nd edn (Wiley-Interscience, 1999). Book; no DOI.
